thread.title: Nvidia: A Buy, But Not Yet - NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA)

author: Nima Abbaszadeh
title: Nvidia: A Buy, But Not Yet - NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA)
text:
(Source: Nvidia website )
Investment Thesis Since the stock of Nvidia Corporation ( NVDA ) peaked back on October 1st near $290, it has fallen by 50%, with roughly two-fifths of the drop coming after the company reported earnings on November 15th. Amidst the wreckage, I look at whether the post-earnings drop was warranted, what a depressed valuation means for NVDA stock, the longer-term prospects of the underlying company, and what the stock looks like from a technical perspective.
Was the Quarter Really That Bad? Looking at the quarter itself, while performance was a bit weak relative to quarters past in terms of growth rates, one would not have thought the Q3 results themselves were enough to justify a 19% post-earnings drop. Non-GAAP EPS came in at $1.84, up 38% Y/Y and beating expectations of $1.71 by $0.13. Similarly, GAAP EPS of $1.97 beat expectations by $0.26, and was up 48% Y/Y.
(Source: Q3 Fiscal 2019 Summary )
Revenues for the quarter were mixed overall: at $3.181B, while good enough for 21% Y/Y growth, they still missed estimates by $60M. Looking at revenues by market platform, performance in most of the company's segments came in with double-digit growth. Revenues for Gaming, the company's largest segment, increased by 13% to $1.764B, but came in short of expectations. The company pointed to excess inventory of mid-range Pascal products that it believes will negatively affect the fourth quarter, and correct in one to two quarters. Datacenter in particular continued what has been a trend of strong positive growth, with revenues of $792M that rose 58% Y/Y. It was the OEM and IP business that was Nvidia's weakest division, with quarterly revenues of $148M that declined 23% Y/Y. This was largely due to the absence of cryptocurrency mining, attributed to the steep declines seen in bitcoin and the broader cryptocurrency market since the asset class peaked in mid-December. This "bitcoin hangover" was the biggest factor in Nvidia's revenue miss, and the prospects for the OEM/IP segment don't look to be improving anytime soon, as the crypto mining business looks to be slowing drastically.
(Source: Q3 Fiscal 2019 Summary )
As I mentioned earlier, while the quarter itself was mixed, it didn't seem bad enough to result in a 19% selloff the day after. So what did lead to the drop?
In the company's Q4 outlook, Nvidia noted that they expect revenues for the quarter to come in at roughly $2.7B, plus or minus two percent. This turned out to be a massive guide down from consensus expectations of $3.4B going into the report, to the tune of around 20.5%. In describing the cause of the weak outlook, the company once again pointed to a weak Gaming segment as it works through its Pascal inventory buildup, as well as the erosion of revenues from OEM and IP amid continued weakness in the cryptocurrency market. Overall, it seemed to be the atrocious revenue guidance for the current quarter that fueled the post-earnings declines, and left a lot of questions to be asked for the near-term.
Why a Lower Valuation Doesn't Matter For most of the last two years, investors were more than happy to pay up at increasingly high valuation multiples for Nvidia's stock, when the company was growing earnings at a breakneck pace. But it's important to remember that markets are forward-thinking mechanisms, in that a company's past performance, no matter how superb, will usually be discounted, and future expectations will usually be given a premium. The difference now is, the company is indicating that it will face near-term headwinds as it works through an oversupply of inventory, and as such the market no longer wants to pay up for a stock with such high multiples when the underlying company isn't backed by strong, consistent growth. This largely explains why a relatively small drop in expected future earnings has caused such a drastic decline in Nvidia's stock price:
NVDA Normalized Diluted EPS (NYSE: TTM ) data by YCharts NVDA data by YCharts With this current environment, NVDA is facing a re-rating of its valuation that falls more in line with that of some of its more traditional semiconductor peers, Intel ( INTC ), Texas Instruments ( TXN ), and Qualcomm ( QCOM ), the latter of which had historically traded in line with the rest of its major peers prior to its debilitating legal dispute with Apple ( AAPL ). This re-rating, in my view, will likely continue to be the case as long as these near-term headwinds persist.
NVDA Normalized Diluted EPS ( TTM ) data by YCharts NVDA PE Ratio ( TTM ) data by YCharts NVDA PS Ratio ( TTM ) data by YCharts I should note that while Nvidia is likely no longer deserving of a P/E multiple in the 40s or 50s, a high 20s to low 30s multiple is very reasonable, considering the company's long-term growth drivers. At a current P/E of just around 20, I view the stock as being too cheap relative to its growth potential; however, this is by no means a signal that it is time to buy the stock, considering that the P/E could yet go lower as the stock continues to drop.
Longer-Term Potential Looking out longer-term, there remain a number of positive growth catalysts and drivers for the company. For one, there is Nvidia's new Turing architecture , recently released in September. The series serves as a successor to the company's Pascal architecture, and its main draw is its combination of real-time ray tracing, advanced shading technology, and AI capabilities. Turing is the first GPU to integrate real-time ray tracing , a rendering technique that allows for more realistic lighting, reflections, and shadows in games. Nvidia remains the definitive leader in the GPU industry over competitors like Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ) and Intel, and innovations like Turing will likely maintain that lead as the gaming industry continues to expand.
(Source: Nvidia 2018 Investor Day Presentation )
(Source: Statista )
Meanwhile, to say that Datacenter has been a strong growth engine for the company would be nothing short of an understatement. Considering that revenues for the division were a mere $97M as recently as Q4 FY16, it's truly mind-boggling to see how far its growth has come since then. The most recent quarter came in with reported revenues of $792M, meaning that revenues for the sector have grown by more than eight times in the span of less than three years. While I doubt that that sort of exponential growth will be here to stay, it's clear that the growth isn't showing signs of stopping as the market for big data remains ever-expanding, with Nvidia estimating a $50B Total Addressable Market , or TAM.
(Source: Nvidia Quarterly Revenue Trend )
On another front, the company also announced a collaboration with a number of Chinese electric car companies earlier this week, in which it will provide them with Nvidia's Xavier AI driving chip and its computing platform in order to develop autonomous vehicle hardware for their cars. These are just a few of the partnerships that Nvidia is developing in the self-driving space, with a long list that includes the likes of Audi, Mercedes-Benz, Toyota, Uber, Volvo, and Volkswagen. While the technology for self-driving vehicles is still in its infancy, Nvidia has established itself as one of the leaders in the race to develop the best technology. It is the company's diversification in applications and advances like these that make Nvidia a unique force in the semiconductor space, and have contributed to the company's rapid acceleration in top- and bottom-line growth over the last few years.
(Source: JP Morgan estimates )
Overall, Nvidia continues to be well-positioned in fast-growing areas like AI, machine learning, autonomous vehicles, datacenters, and gaming; though this news has been well-documented, the stock is now entering a phase where these factors are increasingly being forgotten as near-term pessimism seeps in. I feel, however, that this negative sentiment opens up a longer-term buying opportunity, and in the next section I will look at the stock from a technical point of view to find where this opportunity lies.
When is it Safe to Buy? A Technical Perspective Back in late September/early October, NVDA seemed virtually destined to reach the psychological threshold of $300, with the most recent catalyst for the stock's rise having been the release of the company's new Turing GPUs. When the market pulled back in October, however, NVDA stock was taken down along with it, but to a much greater degree. This was not incredibly surprising, considering the stock's drastically high beta and past history of volatility. However, the October correction in NVDA had led to significant technical damage, as the stock had simultaneously broken below the support of its long-term uptrend and 200-day moving average:
(Source: Stockcharts.com)
Now fast-forward nearly seven weeks from NVDA's peak on October 1st, and the stock has lost 50% of its value, while forming a death cross in the process. Somewhat fitting, I should add, considering it comes just in time for the Black Friday weekend:
(Source: Stockcharts.com)
I had an ominous feeling that this combination of bearish technical indicators in mid-October had marked the end of the bull trend. However, I did not at all expect the degree and the pace at which the stock would fall, though the poor guidance announced with last week's earnings report did a good job of exacerbating the steep drop.
Interestingly, a number of firms have attempted to play these volatile moves in NVDA, with varying degrees of success. Goldman Sachs ( GS ) had actually added NVDA to their " Conviction Buy " list just days after its break of trend, though it was very well clear their assessment didn't take the technical picture into account. In the end they failed to catch the falling knife, and quickly reversed their call post-earnings after admitting they were wrong :
(Source: Stockcharts.com)
Meanwhile, Andrew Left's Citron Research is now long the stock after correctly calling the top (after many previous attempts, mind you), having announced their position on November 20th. However, I still believe they are in too early; from a longer-term perspective, they've certainly managed to initiate their position at a good price, but I don't believe that this is the bottom yet.
So, the question remains: Now what? Well, the stock is currently hanging on to technical support near $140, and while the possibility remains for a near-term bounce there is still too much negative news and sentiment in my view for that support to hold. As such, I would expect the stock to break below and invite an air pocket of selling until the next level of support at ~$120, where I feel is a much better place to buy; this gives an opportunity for the negative news to be digested and priced into the stock at a much stronger level of support. Whether the stock can maintain that support largely remains contingent on whether or not the company can correct its near-term problems regarding inventory buildup.
(Source: Stockcharts.com)
Conclusion To paraphrase a popular investing quip, "If you loved Nvidia at $290, you'll love it even more at $120." I first initiated my long position in NVDA at ~$102 in March of 2017; I've held it all the way up to its peak at $290, and all the way down to where it is now at $145. The rapid ascent had made it a challenge for me to find places to add to my position, but this recent decline opens up a good buying opportunity. The company currently faces short-term challenges, but I believe that its long-term growth story is still very much intact. As such, I would look to buy closer to $120, a level that I feel offers strong technical support and a good long-term entry point.
Disclosure: I am/we are long NVDA, INTC, TXN.
